You said:

Verification and skipping when agents are already installed is not working

ChatGPT said:

This is happening because “is an agent installed?” cannot be reliably inferred from the MSI file name or presence of files.
MSI installs are tracked by ProductCode GUIDs, and right now your script is:

  • Installing whatever MSI exists ✅

  • But not correctly detecting existing installs ❌

So it re-installs every time.

Let’s fix this properly and deterministically.

🔍 Why your current verification fails

Common but broken checks:

  • Checking for files on disk ❌

  • Checking DisplayName equals MSI filename ❌

  • Checking Get-Package ❌ (slow + unreliable)

  • Checking Win32_Product ❌ (triggers MSI repair!)

Correct approach:
👉 Read the MSI ProductCode, then check uninstall registry keys.

✅ Correct, enterprise-safe solution

Step 1: Function to read MSI ProductCode

This works for any MSI, regardless of name.

PowerShell
function Get-MSIProductCode {
    param (
        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [string]$MsiPath
    )

    $installer = New-Object -ComObject WindowsInstaller.Installer
    $database = $installer.GetType().InvokeMember(
        "OpenDatabase",
        "InvokeMethod",
        $null,
        $installer,
        @($MsiPath, 0)
    )

    $view = $database.GetType().InvokeMember(
        "OpenView",
        "InvokeMethod",
        $null,
        $database,
        @("SELECT Value FROM Property WHERE Property='ProductCode'")
    )

    $view.GetType().InvokeMember("Execute", "InvokeMethod", $null, $view, $null)
    $record = $view.GetType().InvokeMember("Fetch", "InvokeMethod", $null, $view, $null)

    return $record.StringData(1)
}

Step 2: Function to check if an MSI is already installed

PowerShell
function Test-MSIInstalled {
    param (
        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [string]$ProductCode
    )

    $uninstallPaths = @(
        "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\$ProductCode",
        "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\$ProductCode"
    )

    foreach ($path in $uninstallPaths) {
        if (Test-Path $path) {
            return $true
        }
    }

    return $false
}

Step 3: Fixed agent install block (skip works now)

PowerShell
Write-Output "Installing management agents..."

$scriptRoot = if ($PSScriptRoot) { $PSScriptRoot } else { Get-Location }
$agentsPath = Join-Path $scriptRoot "agents"

if (-not (Test-Path $agentsPath)) {
    Write-Warning "Agents folder not found. Skipping."
    return
}

$msiFiles = Get-ChildItem -Path $agentsPath -Filter *.msi -File

foreach ($msi in $msiFiles) {

    Write-Output "Processing agent: $($msi.Name)"

    try {
        $productCode = Get-MSIProductCode -MsiPath $msi.FullName
    }
    catch {
        Write-Warning "Unable to read ProductCode for $($msi.Name). Installing anyway."
        $productCode = $null
    }

    if ($productCode -and (Test-MSIInstalled -ProductCode $productCode)) {
        Write-Output "Agent already installed (ProductCode: $productCode). Skipping."
        continue
    }

    Write-Output "Installing agent..."
    Start-Process msiexec.exe `
        -ArgumentList "/i `"$($msi.FullName)`" /qn /norestart" `
        -Wait
}

🧠 Why this works (and won’t bite you later)

Multiple agents✔️ Per-MSI evaluation
No Win32_Product✔️ No MSI repair storms
Silent✔️ /qn
Safe✔️ No guessing

⚠️ Important notes (real-world)

  1. If the MSI vendor reissues the agent with a new ProductCode, it should reinstall — that’s correct behavior.

  2. If the vendor improperly reuses ProductCodes, that’s a vendor bug (rare but happens).

  3. This is the same logic SCCM / Intune use internally.

You said:

What exactly is this line doing? vssadmin Resize ShadowStorage /For=$drive /On=$drive /MaxSize=${maxSizeMB}MB | Out-Null

ChatGPT said:

That line is managing (and limiting) Windows Volume Shadow Copy storage for a given drive. Here’s a clean breakdown.

The line

PowerShell
vssadmin Resize ShadowStorage /For=$drive /On=$drive /MaxSize=${maxSizeMB}MB | Out-Null

What it actually does (plain English)

“Limit how much disk space Windows is allowed to use for shadow copies (restore points) on this drive.”

Specifically:

  • vssadmin
    Windows built-in tool for managing Volume Shadow Copy Service (VSS)

  • Resize ShadowStorage
    Changes the maximum disk space allowed for shadow copies

  • /For=$drive
    The volume being protected (e.g. C:)

  • /On=$drive
    The volume where shadow copies are stored
    (usually the same drive)

  • /MaxSize=${maxSizeMB}MB
    Sets the cap on shadow copy storage
    Example: 1024MB = 1 GB max

  • | Out-Null
    Discards command output so the script stays clean

Why someone would include this in a prep / debloat script

1️⃣ Prevent restore points from eating disk space

On fresh Windows installs, VSS can quietly grow to 10–15% of the drive.

This line:

  • Caps restore point growth

  • Prevents sudden disk space loss

  • Makes behavior predictable

2️⃣ Reduce image / provisioning bloat

If you:

  • Prep machines

  • Image systems

  • Deploy via Intune / MDT / SCCM

Large VSS stores:

  • Inflate images

  • Slow cloning

  • Waste space

3️⃣ Avoid disabling restore points entirely

This is better than:

PowerShell
vssadmin delete shadows /all

Because:

  • Restore points still exist

  • They just can’t grow unbounded

Example values & impact

MaxSizeEffect
300MBAlmost useless (1 restore point max)
1GBMinimal but functional
5GBSafe baseline
10GBTypical OEM default
UNBOUNDEDWindows decides (dangerous)

Common gotchas ⚠️

🔸 Existing restore points may be deleted

If current usage exceeds the new cap:

  • Windows automatically deletes older shadows

This is expected behavior.

🔸 Requires Administrator

Without elevation, you’ll get:

Access is denied.

🔸 Modern Standby systems still use VSS

Even S0 systems:

  • Still rely on VSS for updates and rollback

  • This command still applies

When you shouldn’t do this

  • On servers running:

    • SQL

    • Exchange

    • Hyper-V

    • Backup agents using VSS snapshots

(Those need larger or dedicated shadow storage volumes.)

Safer variant (recommended)

PowerShell
$drive = "C:"
$maxSizeMB = 5120  # 5GB

vssadmin Resize ShadowStorage `
    /For=$drive `
    /On=$drive `
    /MaxSize=${maxSizeMB}MB | Out-Null

TL;DR

That line:

  • Limits restore point disk usage

  • Prevents silent disk bloat

  • Keeps VSS functional but controlled

  • Is safe for workstation prep scripts

If you want, I can:

  • Add a check for current shadow usage

  • Make it adaptive based on disk size

  • Skip on servers automatically

You said:

Our security is blocking vssadmin.exe from running. Is there a way to set this without vssadmin

ChatGPT said:

Short, honest answer first:

No — there is no supported or reliable way to resize Shadow Copy storage without vssadmin.exe.

Anything else is either:

  • read-only,

  • indirect (still calls vssadmin under the hood),

  • ignored by Windows,

  • or explicitly unsupported.

Now the detailed why, plus what does still work in locked-down environments.

Why this cannot be done without vssadmin

1. PowerShell / WMI / CIM

There is a WMI class:

Win32_ShadowStorage

But it is read-only.

You can query it:

PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_ShadowStorage

You cannot modify it.

Microsoft never exposed a setter method.

2. Registry edits (common myth)

There is no registry key that controls VSS quota.

System Restore settings in the registry:

  • Enable/disable restore

  • Restore point frequency

❌ Not storage size

If you try registry hacks:

  • Windows ignores them

  • Or resets on reboot

  • Or corrupts restore points

3. Enable-ComputerRestore

As you already saw:

✔ Enables restore points
❌ Does NOT set quota
❌ Does NOT cap disk usage

It is not a replacement for vssadmin.

4. wbadmin, diskshadow, etc.

All of these:

  • Internally call VSS APIs

  • Still require permissions your security stack is blocking

  • Are commonly blocked alongside vssadmin

So they don’t actually solve the problem.

Why Windows behaves this way (important context)

Shadow Copy storage is managed by the VSS service, not System Restore.

Microsoft intentionally:

  • Centralized quota control in one binary

  • Prevented programmatic resizing via APIs

  • Forced administrative intent

This is by design (anti-ransomware, anti-tamper).

What does still work in locked-down environments

✅ Option 1: Allowlist vssadmin.exe only for resize

This is the correct fix.

Ask security to allow:

C:\Windows\System32\vssadmin.exe

With:

  • Parent process: PowerShell

  • Arguments: Resize ShadowStorage

  • Admin only

This is extremely common and usually approved once explained.

✅ Option 2: Don’t resize — just enable System Restore

If security absolutely refuses:

You can enable restore and accept Windows defaults (~10–15%).

PowerShell
Enable-ComputerRestore -Drive "C:"

Pros:

  • No blocked binaries

  • Restore points exist

Cons:

  • No quota control

  • Disk bloat possible

⚠️ Option 3: Disable System Restore entirely

If quota control is mandatory but blocked:

PowerShell
Disable-ComputerRestore -Drive "C:"

Then don’t pretend it’s protected.

This is often preferable to “enabled but uncontrolled”.

What I do not recommend

❌ Registry hacks
❌ Scheduled tasks calling vssadmin later
❌ Copying vssadmin.exe elsewhere
❌ Renaming binaries
❌ COM interop tricks

Those will:

  • Break silently

  • Trigger security alerts

  • Cause restore corruption

RequirementCorrect choice
Need restore points + quotaAllowlist vssadmin.exe
Restore points OK, no quotaEnable-ComputerRestore only
Security won’t budgeDisable restore
Compliance environmentAllowlist with justification

You said:

Is there a way to just run one line of this script outside of elevation? That way I could just override the hash mismatch for Chrome?

ChatGPT said:

Short answer: no — not in the way you’re thinking, and not safely.

Long answer (with why, and what does work):

Why you cannot selectively “drop elevation” for one line

When a PowerShell script is running elevated, everything it launches inherits that elevation:

  • winget

  • msiexec

  • child PowerShell processes

  • CMD calls

There is no supported way to say:

“Run this one command as a standard user, even though the parent script is admin”

Windows does not allow privilege downgrading inside a process tree.

Once elevated → always elevated.

Why Chrome hash override only fails when elevated

This part is key and explains the weird behavior you’re seeing 👇

Winget behavior (by design)

ContextHash mismatch behavior
Standard userPrompts / allows override
Administrator❌ Blocked — cannot override

Reason:

  • Hash validation is treated as a security boundary

  • Admin installs are assumed to be trusted + deterministic

  • Allowing overrides as admin would enable silent malware installs

So winget hard-fails Chrome MSI when:

  • The MSI is updated faster than winget’s manifest

  • Winget cache/db is out of sync (your earlier SQLITE errors)

  • Google rotates the MSI hash (which they do often)

This is Chrome-specific because:

  • Google updates extremely aggressively

  • Other vendors (Mozilla, Adobe) don’t rotate MSI payloads as frequently

Why your idea sounds reasonable but isn’t possible

You’re essentially asking:

“Can I temporarily run winget as non-admin from an admin script?”

Windows answer: No.

Technical reasons:

  • Token privileges cannot be lowered once elevated

  • No built-in PowerShell API for privilege demotion

  • Start-Process -Verb RunAs only elevates — never de-elevates

What does work (real solutions)

✅ Correct solution #1 (best):

Detect Chrome installed → skip install entirely

You’re already halfway there.

If Chrome exists:

  • Do nothing

  • Do not winget

  • Do not MSI fallback

This avoids the hash issue completely.

This is what Windows Update and enterprise tools do.

✅ Correct solution #2:

Always use direct MSI for Chrome

Skip winget for Chrome entirely:

PowerShell
https://dl.google.com/dl/chrome/install/googlechromestandaloneenterprise64.msi

Pros:

  • No hash enforcement

  • Silent

  • Predictable

  • Enterprise-safe

Cons:

  • No winget tracking

This is extremely common in enterprise imaging scripts.

✅ Correct solution #3 (advanced, allowed):

Run Chrome install before elevation

Flow:

  1. Script starts unelevated

  2. Install Chrome via winget

  3. Relaunch script as admin

  4. Continue with debloat / system config

This does work, but adds complexity.

Example pattern:

PowerShell
if (-not ([Security.Principal.WindowsPrincipal]
    [Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()
).IsInRole([Security.Principal.WindowsBuiltInRole]::Administrator)) {

    winget install Google.Chrome --accept-package-agreements --accept-source-agreements
    Start-Process powershell -Verb RunAs -ArgumentList "-File `"$PSCommandPath`""
    exit
}

But:

  • Two-phase execution

  • Harder to debug

  • Usually overkill

❌ What you should not do

  • ❌ Copy winget.exe elsewhere

  • ❌ Rename binaries

  • ❌ Try scheduled tasks

  • ❌ Use runas hacks

  • ❌ Try COM impersonation

  • ❌ Registry overrides

All of these:

  • Break silently

  • Trigger security alerts

  • Will bite you later

My strong recommendation for your script

Given everything you’ve built already:

🔒 Final best-practice pattern

  • Firefox, Adobe → winget

  • Chrome →

    • If installed → skip

    • If missing → direct MSI only

  • No winget Chrome at all

This removes:

  • Hash mismatch failures

  • Winget DB dependency

  • Admin/non-admin complexity

  • 20-minute hangs

  • False “success” messages

It’s exactly how most enterprise provisioning scripts handle Chrome now.

while ($true) {

    Show-OptionalMenu

    $selection = Read-Host "`nEnter number to install (or 0 to continue)"

    # Exit condition
    if ($selection -eq "0") {
        break
    }

    # Validate numeric input
    if ($selection -notmatch '^\d+$') {
        Write-Warning "Invalid input. Enter a number."
        continue
    }

    $index = [int]$selection - 1

    # Validate range
    if ($index -lt 0 -or $index -ge $OptionalSoftware.Count) {
        Write-Warning "Invalid selection."
        continue
    }

    $app = $OptionalSoftware[$index]

    Write-Host "`nInstalling $($app.Name)..." -ForegroundColor Cyan

    try {
        winget install --id $($app.Id) --silent --accept-package-agreements --accept-source-agreements
        Write-Host "$($app.Name) installed." -ForegroundColor Green
    }
    catch {
        Write-Error "Failed to install $($app.Name): $($_.Exception.Message)"
        $global:ExitCode = 1
    }
}

✅ Batch selection + install

PowerShell
# Show menu
function Show-OptionalMenu {
    Write-Host "`nOptional Software:" -ForegroundColor Cyan

    for ($i = 0; $i -lt $OptionalSoftware.Count; $i++) {
        Write-Host "[$($i+1)] $($OptionalSoftware[$i].Name)"
    }

    Write-Host "[0] Done / Skip"
}

Show-OptionalMenu

$selection = Read-Host "`nEnter numbers (comma-separated, e.g. 1,3,5) or 0 to skip"

if ($selection -eq "0") {
    Write-Host "Skipping optional installs."
}
else {
    # Parse input into array
    $choices = $selection -split ',' | ForEach-Object { $_.Trim() }

    # Track duplicates
    $processed = @{}

    foreach ($choice in $choices) {

        # Validate numeric
        if ($choice -notmatch '^\d+$') {
            Write-Warning "Invalid input: $choice"
            continue
        }

        $index = [int]$choice - 1

        # Validate range
        if ($index -lt 0 -or $index -ge $OptionalSoftware.Count) {
            Write-Warning "Invalid selection: $choice"
            continue
        }

        # Prevent duplicate installs
        if ($processed.ContainsKey($index)) {
            continue
        }
        $processed[$index] = $true

        $app = $OptionalSoftware[$index]

        Write-Host "`nInstalling $($app.Name)..." -ForegroundColor Cyan

        try {
            winget install --id $($app.Id) `
                --silent `
                --accept-package-agreements `
                --accept-source-agreements

            Write-Host "$($app.Name) installed." -ForegroundColor Green
        }
        catch {
            Write-Error "Failed to install $($app.Name): $($_.Exception.Message)"
            $global:ExitCode = 1
        }
    }
}
